arXiv:1705.07424v1 [math.AP] 21 May 2017

Diffusive Wave in the Low Mach Limit for Non-Viscous and Heat-Conductive Gas Thanks: Supported by the Construct Program of the Key Discipline in Hunan Province. email: lyc9009@sina.cn

Yechi Liu Affiliation: Key Laboratory of High Performance Computing and Stochastic Information Processing Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Hunan Normal University, Changsha, Hunan 410081, P. R. China

Abstract The low Mach number limit for one-dimensional non-isentropic compressible Navier-Stokes system without viscosity is investigated, where the density and temperature have different asymptotic states at far fields. It is proved that the solution of the system converges to a nonlinear diffusion wave globally in time as Mach number goes to zero. It is remarked that the velocity of diffusion wave is proportional with the variation of temperature. Furthermore, it is shown that the solution of compressible Navier-Stokes system also has the same phenomenon when Mach number is suitably small.

Keywords: Compressible Navier-Stokes equations, low Mach limit, nonlinear diffusion wave

1. Introduction

The one-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes system in Lagrangian coordinates reads

vt−ux=0,\displaystyle v_{t}-u_{x}=0,
ut+Px=(μ​uxv)x,\displaystyle u_{t}+P_{x}=(\mu\frac{u_{x}}{v})_{x}, (1.1)
(e+u22)t+(P​u)x=(κ​θxv+μ​u​uxv)x,\displaystyle(e+\frac{u^{2}}{2})_{t}+(Pu)_{x}=(\kappa\frac{\theta_{x}}{v}+\mu\frac{uu_{x}}{v})_{x},

where the unknown functions vv, uu and θ\theta represent the specific volume, velocity and temperature, respectively, while μ>0\mu>0 and κ>0\kappa>0 denote the viscosity and heat conductivity coefficients respectively. Here, we consider the perfect gas, so that the pressure function PP and the internal function ee are given by

P=R​θv,ande=cv​θ+c​o​n​s​t.,P=R\frac{\theta}{v},\quad\textrm{and}\quad e=c_{v}\theta+const.,

where the parameters R>0R>0 and cv>0c_{v}>0 are the gas constant and heat capacity at the constant volume respectively. For simplicity, we assume μ\mu and κ\kappa are constants, and normalize R=1R=1 and cv=1c_{v}=1.

The low Mach limit is an important and interesting problem in fluid dynamics. The first result is due to Klainerman and Majda [16, 17], in which they proved the incompressible limit of the isentropic Euler equations to the incompressible Euler equations for local smooth solutions. In [1], Alazard showed the incompressible limit for Navier-Stokes equations in the whole space. Note that in [1], the solutions have the same states at the far fields.

Recently, Huang et.al. [13] began to study the case that the solutions have different end states and found that the solutions of compressible Navier-Stokes equations converge to a nonlinear diffusion wave solution globally in time as Mach number goes to zero, which is related to the thermal creep flow. That is, the flow in diffusion wave is only driven by the variation of temperature. This phenomenon is quite different from the constant case. Since the diffusion wave is independent of the viscosity μ=0\mu=0, we conjecture that the result of [13] is still valid without viscosity, that is μ=0\mu=0 in the system (1.1). Precisely speaking, we consider the non-viscous and heat-conductive gas in the following system

vt−ux=0,\displaystyle v_{t}-u_{x}=0,
ut+Px=0,\displaystyle u_{t}+P_{x}=0, (1.2)
(θ+u22)t+(P​u)x=(κ​θxv)x,\displaystyle(\theta+\frac{u^{2}}{2})_{t}+(Pu)_{x}=(\kappa\frac{\theta_{x}}{v})_{x},

where the only difference with the system (1.1) is that μ=0\mu=0. We will prove that the solution of system (1.2) converges to a nonlinear diffusion wave solution globally in time as Mach number tends to zero. Moreover, as the Mach number is suitably small, the flow is only driven by the variation of temperature.

Let ε\varepsilon be the compressibility parameter, which represents the maximum Mach number of the fluid. As in [26], we set

t→ε​t,x→x,u→ε​u,μ→ε​μ,κ→ε​κ.t\rightarrow\varepsilon t,\quad x\rightarrow x,\quad u\rightarrow\varepsilon u,\quad\mu\rightarrow\varepsilon\mu,\quad\kappa\rightarrow\varepsilon\kappa.

By the above changes of variables, system (1.2) is written as

vtε−uxε=0,\displaystyle v_{t}^{\varepsilon}-u_{x}^{\varepsilon}=0,
utε+1ε2​Pxε=0,\displaystyle u_{t}^{\varepsilon}+\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{2}}P^{\varepsilon}_{x}=0, (1.3)
[θε+12​(ε​uε)2]t+(Pε​uε)x=κ​(θxεvε)x.\displaystyle[\theta^{\varepsilon}+\frac{1}{2}(\varepsilon u^{\varepsilon})^{2}]_{t}+(P^{\varepsilon}u^{\varepsilon})_{x}=\kappa(\frac{\theta_{x}^{\varepsilon}}{v^{\varepsilon}})_{x}.

As ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0, the limit of solutions of (1.3) is called the low Mach limit [16, 17]. Similar to [1, 13, 26], we assume that the pressure is a small perturbation of a given constant state P¯>0\bar{P}>0, i.e.

P=P¯+O⁡(ε),P=\bar{P}+O(\varepsilon), (1.4)

and without loss of generality, we further assume P¯\bar{P} to be 11. Formally, as the Mach number goes to zero, the limit system of (1.3) is

(2​u−κ​Tx)x=0,ρ=T−1,\displaystyle(2u-\kappa T_{x})_{x}=0,\,\,\rho=T^{-1},
ut+πx=0,\displaystyle u_{t}+\pi_{x}=0, (1.5)
θt+ux=κ​(θxv)x,\displaystyle\theta_{t}+u_{x}=\kappa(\frac{\theta_{x}}{v})_{x},

and

vt−ux=0,v_{t}-u_{x}=0,

in which πx\pi_{x} is the limit of 1ε2​Pxε\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{2}}P^{\varepsilon}_{x}.

We will study the low Mach limit and what happens in the limiting process when the background is not constant state, i.e.

(vε,θε)​(x,t)→(v±,θ±),as​x→±∞,with​θ−v−=θ+v+,(v^{\varepsilon},\theta^{\varepsilon})(x,t)\rightarrow(v_{\pm},\theta_{\pm}),\quad{\rm as}\,x\rightarrow\pm\infty,\quad{\rm with}\,\,\frac{\theta_{-}}{v_{-}}=\frac{\theta_{+}}{v_{+}}, (1.6)

where θ−\theta_{-} may not be equal to θ+\theta_{+}. Following [13], we shall construct a spacial diffusive wave (v¯,u¯,θ¯,π¯)(\bar{v},\bar{u},\bar{\theta},\bar{\pi}) of (1.5) by choosing

Finally let us outline the proof of Theorem 1. Since there is no viscosity in (1.3)2, the system (1.3) is less dissipative compared with the system (1.1). It is not trivial to obtain the higher order estimates. Indeed, even for the basic energy estimate, the derivative estimate for ψy2\psi_{y}^{2} is missing, see (2.13) below. To prove Theorem 1, we first obtain the estimates for ‖ζy‖H1\|\zeta_{y}\|_{H^{1}} though the basic energy. Then, by the compensation method (cf. [19]), we control simultaneously the estimates for ‖(ϕy,ψy)‖H1\|(\phi_{y},\psi_{y})\|_{H^{1}} by ‖ζy‖H1\|\zeta_{y}\|_{H^{1}}. Motivated by [13], a new type differential inequality is essentially used to obtain the desired a priori estimates.

The rest of this paper will be arranged in the following way. Section 2 is devoted to the details of the proof, in which the energy estimates will be used, while Section 3 is Appendix to prove an approximation of a self-similar solution, which will be used in the proof of the main results.

2. Proof of Theorem 1

For simplicity, we omit the superscript ε\varepsilon of the variables in this section.

2.1 Reformulation of the System
